docs.title: phu - Phage Utilities
docs.text:
A modular toolkit for viral genomics workflows

phu (phage utilities) is a command-line toolkit for working with phage and other viral sequences. Each command answers one common question about your contigs, from "which of them carry this protein family?" to "which of them belong to the same species?", and records what it did so the result can be reproduced.

  • One install, no external programs for searching: gene prediction, HMM searches and alignments run inside phu (only cluster calls vclust).
  • Reference databases included: Pfam, KOfam, PHROG, ECOD, dbCAN and the CheckAMG tables come as one pinned bundle that installs itself on first use.
  • Reproducible: every run writes the exact query, thresholds, database versions and file checksums to a .phu/ folder beside its results.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
mamba create -n phu bioconda::phu
mamba activate phu
phu --help

The databases download on first use (about 2.9 GB). On a cluster, install them once on a shared filesystem first; see Databases.

docs.title: What do you want to do?
docs.text: I want to… Command Example Find contigs that carry given protein families screen phu screen -i contigs.fa PF00589 phrog_2 ecod:2004.1 Find contigs carrying relatives of proteins I already have jack phu jack -i contigs.fa seeds.faa Look up PHROG families by name or function phrogs phu phrogs search "tail fiber" Find putative auxiliary viral genes (AVGs) avger phu avger -i viral-contigs.fa Dereplicate, or group genomes into vOTUs, genera or species cluster phu cluster --mode votu -i genomes.fa Tidy vContact lineage predictions normalize-lineage Install the databases ahead of time dbs prepare phu dbs prepare Free disk space clean phu clean --cache

docs.title: screen: find contigs by their protein families
docs.text:
Predicts the proteins of your contigs, searches them with profile HMMs, and keeps the contigs that match. Queries can be your own HMM files or families named from the databases: Pfam (PF00589), KOfam (K00001), PHROG (phrog_216), ECOD domains at any level of its hierarchy (ecod:2004.1), dbCAN CAZymes (GH128) or a dbCAN PUL (PUL0621). Each database's own cutoffs apply; combine queries with --combine-mode any|all|threshold.

phu screen -i assembly.fasta --combine-mode all capsid.hmm portal.hmm

Screen guide → · How hits are judged →

docs.title: jack: find relatives of seed proteins
docs.text:
Builds a profile from each seed protein by iterative search (pyhmmer.jackhmmer) and keeps the contigs that carry relatives. Seeds can be your own proteins or PHROG families.

phu jack -i assembly.fasta marker_seeds.faa --combine-mode all
phu jack -i assembly.fasta --phrog alias:portal

Jack guide →

docs.title: phrogs: find PHROG families by name
docs.text:
Turns names into PHROG identifiers for screen and jack: curated aliases (alias:mcp, alias:terl), functional categories (category:tail) or a forgiving search of the annotations.

phu phrogs search "tail fiber"
phu screen -i assembly.fasta $(phu phrogs resolve alias:mcp alias:terl --ids-only)

PHROG lookup guide →

docs.title: avger: auxiliary viral genes
docs.text:
Annotates the proteins of viral contigs against Pfam, KOfam and PHROG, and applies CheckAMG-style rules to flag putative auxiliary metabolic, physiology and regulatory genes.

phu avger -i viral-contigs.fasta -o phu-avger

AVG guide →

docs.title: cluster: group sequences
docs.text:
Clusters viral sequences with vclust in four modes: dereplication, votu, genus (complete genomes, tANI ≥ 70%) and species (tANI ≥ 95%).

phu cluster --mode votu -i viral-genomes.fasta

Clustering guide →

docs.title: normalize-lineage: tidy vContact lineages
docs.text: Normalizes vContact lineage predictions while keeping the input table's columns. Lineage guide →

docs.title: dbs and clean: databases and disk space
docs.text:
phu dbs prepare installs the database bundle ahead of time; phu clean lists what phu keeps between runs (cached protein predictions, installed databases) and removes it on request.

phu dbs prepare                          # install the databases now
phu dbs prepare --bundle phu-db.tar.gz   # from a pre-downloaded copy
phu clean                                # show what phu keeps and its size
phu clean --cache                        # remove cached predictions

Set PHU_DB_FOLDER to a shared folder so every job reuses one install. Databases → · Cache →

docs.text:

    Zielezinski A, Gudyś A, Barylski J, Siminski K, Rozwalak P, Dutilh BE, Deorowicz S. Ultrafast and accurate sequence alignment and clustering of viral genomes. Nat Methods. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-025-02701-7

  • FAMSA and pyfamsa: A multiple sequence aligner for large protein families, and its Python bindings.

    Deorowicz, S., Debudaj-Grabysz, A., & Gudyś, A. (2016). FAMSA: Fast and accurate multiple sequence alignment of huge protein families. Scientific Reports, 6, 33964. https://doi.org/10.1038/srep33964

  • trimAl and pytrimal: Automated alignment trimming, and its Python bindings.

    Capella-Gutiérrez, S., Silla-Martínez, J. M., & Gabaldón, T. (2009). trimAl: a tool for automated alignment trimming in large-scale phylogenetic analyses. Bioinformatics, 25(15), 1972–1973. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btp348

  • Prodigal: A gene prediction tool for prokaryotic genomes.

    Hyatt, D., Chen, G. L., LoCascio, P. F., Land, M. L., Larimer, F. W., & Hauser, L. J. (2010). Prodigal: prokaryotic gene recognition and translation initiation site identification. BMC bioinformatics, 11(1), 119. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2105-11-119

    Larralde, M., (2022). Pyrodigal: Python bindings and interface to Prodigal, an efficient method for gene prediction in prokaryotes. Journal of Open Source Software, 7(72), 4296, https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.04296

    Eddy, S. R. (2011). Accelerated Profile HMM Searches. PLoS Computational Biology, 7(10), e1002195. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1002195

  • pyHMMER: Python bindings for HMMER.

    Larralde, M., & Zeller, G. (2023). PyHMMER: a Python library binding to HMMER for efficient sequence analysis. Bioinformatics, 39(5). https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btad214

docs.title: Cache Handling
docs.text: Predicting proteins is often the slowest step of a run. phu screen, phu jack and phu avger keep the predicted proteins in a cache, so a second run on the same contigs, with different queries or thresholds, starts straight at the search.

docs.title: What the cache stores
docs.text: The cache stores the translated protein FASTA generated from the input contigs. Search-specific inputs such as HMM files, seed markers, combine mode, and output folder are not part of the cache key.

docs.title: When the cache is reused
docs.text:
The cached proteins are reused when all prediction inputs are the same:

  • the same contigs (same file content);
  • the same --mode, --min-protein-len-aa and, in phu jack, --min-gene-len;
  • the same --ttable, when you give one.

docs.title: When the cache is rebuilt
docs.text:
The cache is invalidated and rebuilt when any of these prediction inputs change:

  • --mode
  • --min-gene-len in phu jack
  • --min-protein-len-aa
  • an explicit --ttable

Without --ttable, pyrodigal-gv picks the genetic code of each contig in meta mode, and that choice is part of the cached result.

docs.title: How to control it
docs.text:
Cache behavior is controlled by environment variables:

  • PHU_CACHE=off disables caching and always recomputes proteins.
  • PHU_CACHE_DIR overrides the cache location.
  • If PHU_CACHE_DIR is not set, phu uses an XDG-style cache directory under your home cache path.

You can also remove all cached predictions explicitly:

phu clean            # list what phu keeps and its size
phu clean --cache    # remove the prediction cache

--cache removes the full cache directory resolved by PHU_CACHE_DIR (or the default cache path). phu clean --dbs removes the installed database bundle and partial downloads, after asking, since they must be downloaded again; --all does both, and --dry-run only lists.

docs.title: Database index files
docs.text: The cache directory can also hold a phu-db-derived/ folder. PHU builds a small index and per-model files for each reference database the first time it is queried. They normally sit beside the database files; when the database install is read-only for you, PHU keeps them here instead. phu clean --cache removes them too, and they are rebuilt on the next database query. See Databases and Provenance.

docs.title: Practical cases
docs.text:
• Changing only HMM files in screen reuses the cached proteins.
  • Changing only seed markers in jack reuses the cached proteins.
  • Changing the protein-length filter rebuilds the cache, which is expected because it changes the predicted protein set.

docs.title: Citation
docs.text:
CITATION.cff is the source of truth for PHU citation metadata. This documentation describes the 0.9.1 release.

For a published study, cite the immutable PHU release used for the analysis and record its version in the run manifest. Use the Zenodo concept DOI for software-level references that are not tied to one release. The release DOI must come from the corresponding release metadata and must not be inferred from this development page.

PHU analyses should also cite the external tools and databases actually used, including their versions or immutable releases. The relevant scientific citations and database provenance belong in the run manifest alongside the PHU version.

See the repository's CITATION.cff for the machine-readable author and software metadata.

For the databases, cite the phu-db bundle version recorded in .phu/ and the upstream databases you relied on; see Databases and Provenance.

docs.title: Databases and Provenance
docs.text:
phu searches six reference databases: Pfam, KOfam, dbCAN, PHROG, ECOD and the CheckAMG tables for auxiliary viral genes (AVG). They come as one pinned, checksummed bundle, phu-db, which phu installs the first time a command needs it. You can also install it ahead of time with phu dbs prepare.

Command Uses phu screen Pfam, KOfam, PHROG, ECOD, dbCAN phu jack --phrog PHROG (as seeds) phu phrogs PHROG annotations phu avger Pfam, KOfam, PHROG and the AVG tables phu cluster, phu normalize-lineage none

docs.title: Installing ahead of time
docs.text:
phu dbs prepare

This downloads the bundle from Zenodo, verifies it and installs it, then prints where it is and which upstream releases it holds. It is optional, but useful on a login node before submitting jobs, so that compute jobs neither download nor wait for each other. If the bundle is already installed, the command only checks it and returns.

Option Effect --bundle PATH Install from a pre-downloaded phu-db.tar.gz instead of downloading (same as PHU_DB_BUNDLE). --verify Re-hash every installed file and reinstall if any check fails (same as PHU_DB_VERIFY=1). --connections N Download N parts of the bundle at once, from 1 to 16 (default 8; same as PHU_DB_CONNECTIONS).

The bundle always holds all six databases, so database names given to phu dbs prepare are accepted and ignored.

docs.title: What happens on first use
docs.text:
phu dbs prepare, or the first database-backed command if you skipped it:

  1. Checks free disk space. The install needs about 20 GB free while it runs: the 2.9 GB download plus the 16.2 GB of databases. Once the download is removed and the fast-loading models are built, it takes about 21 GB.
  2. Downloads phu-db.tar.gz (about 2.9 GB) from Zenodo, or uses a local copy if PHU_DB_BUNDLE is set.
  3. Verifies the tarball's exact size and SHA-256 against the values pinned in this PHU release. A mismatch stops the install; nothing is used.
  4. Unpacks it after checking every member (no links, devices or paths that escape the install folder), then verifies every database file's size, SHA-256 and record count.
  5. Moves the finished tree into place in one step, so an interrupted install never leaves a half-installed database behind.

PHU prints what it downloads, how large it is and where it goes. The bundle is downloaded in several parts at once and an interrupted download continues where each part stopped. While it downloads, a terminal shows a spinner with a progress bar, the speed and the time left; a log file (for example a SLURM job's) gets one line per 10%. Later runs only check file sizes, and line counts of the small tables, which takes a moment, and do not download again.

If several jobs start at once against the same database folder, the first one installs and the others wait for it, then reuse its result.

docs.title: Where databases are installed
docs.text:
Setting Location PHU_DB_FOLDER set $PHU_DB_FOLDER otherwise, XDG_DATA_HOME set $XDG_DATA_HOME/phu/db otherwise ~/.local/share/phu/db

Inside that folder:

phu-db/
  phu-db-0.4.0/
    installed.json        # source, tarball SHA-256, install time
    phu-db.json           # the bundle manifest: upstream URLs, digests, steps
    pfam/  profiles.hmm
    kofam/ profiles.hmm, ko_list.tsv
    dbcan/ profiles.hmm, family_substrate.tsv, pul_rules.tsv
    avg/   v_scores.tsv, positive_{amg,apg,areg}.tsv, filters_{amg,apg,areg}.tsv
    phrog/ profiles.hmm, msa_a3m.tar.gz, annotations.tsv
    ecod/  profiles.hmm, msa_a3m.tar.gz, sequences.fa, families.tsv, domains.tsv

When a new PHU release pins a newer bundle, it installs the new version beside the old one. PHU never deletes other versions, because another PHU release sharing the folder may still be using them; remove an old phu-db-<version>/ folder yourself once nothing needs it.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variable Effect PHU_DB_FOLDER Install root (see above). PHU_DB_BUNDLE Path to a pre-downloaded phu-db.tar.gz. It is verified exactly like a download, and PHU never deletes it. PHU_DB_CONNECTIONS How many parts of the bundle to download at once, from 1 to 16 (default 8). Zenodo limits the speed of each connection, so several parts at once download several times faster. Use 1 for a single connection. PHU_DB_VERIFY=1 Re-hash every installed file of every database on this run instead of checking sizes only, and discard the indexes and per-model files PHU built from them (they are rebuilt on next use). Reads about 16 GB, so use it when you suspect corruption, not routinely. A failed check reinstalls.

docs.title: Offline and HPC use
docs.text:
Compute nodes often have no internet access, or many jobs would download the same bundle at once. Download it once and point PHU at it:

# On a node with internet access: get phu-db.tar.gz for phu-db-0.4.0 from
# https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19503347 (the page lists every version).
export PHU_DB_FOLDER=/shared/project/phu-db      # on a shared filesystem
phu dbs prepare --bundle /shared/project/phu-db.tar.gz   # installs once
phu screen PF00001 -i contigs.fna                 # every job reuses the install

Install once on a shared filesystem and every job reuses the same tree. The install lock is released as soon as a job exits, even if it is killed. On network filesystems without flock support, PHU uses a lock directory instead. A running install re-stamps it every minute, and PHU clears one that a killed job left without a stamp for six hours.

PHU builds a small index and per-model files for each database the first time it is queried, and keeps them beside the database files. phu dbs prepare also writes a binary copy of each model file phu avger searches (profiles.h3m, about 5 GB for Pfam, KOfam and PHROG together), which loads in seconds where the text file takes minutes. Building them takes a few minutes and is shown as its own step. If you skip phu dbs prepare, the first phu avger run builds them, as a step named "Building fast-loading models (one time)". The copies are rebuilt automatically if the database or pyhmmer changes; if they cannot be written, PHU reads the text files instead. If the install is read-only for you (for example one a colleague or an administrator installed), PHU keeps them in your own cache folder instead (PHU_CACHE_DIR, default ~/.cache/phu), so a shared read-only install works as is.

If the tarball does not match the version this PHU release pins, PHU refuses it and says so. Download the version named in the error.

docs.title: What the bundle contains
docs.text:
phu-db-0.4.0 contains these pinned upstream releases. PHU records them in each run's provenance.

Database Used by Upstream release Files pfam screen, avger Pfam 37.0 (CC0-1.0) profiles.hmm (21,979 models) kofam screen, avger KOfam, genome.jp archive 2026-07-02 profiles.hmm, ko_list.tsv (KO thresholds) dbcan screen dbCAN HMMdb V15; dbCAN-PUL substrate table 12-12-2023; dbCAN-PUL workbook snapshot of 2026-09-30 profiles.hmm, family_substrate.tsv, pul_rules.tsv avg avger CheckAMG v1.1.1 reference tables V-scores, AMG/APG/AReG positive tables and filter tables phrog screen, jack, phrogs, avger PHROGs v4 (CC-BY-4.0) profiles.hmm (38,880 models), msa_a3m.tar.gz (38,880 alignments), annotations.tsv ecod screen ECOD v295.2, F70 representatives (CC-BY-4.0) profiles.hmm (32,041 models), msa_a3m.tar.gz (32,041 alignments), sequences.fa, families.tsv, domains.tsv

PHROGs is published as HH-suite profiles and MMseqs2 databases, which HMMER cannot search. The PHROG models in the bundle were built from the official per-PHROG alignments with pyhmmer, using the default hmmbuild settings, one model per PHROG, named phrog_1 to phrog_38880.

phrog/msa_a3m.tar.gz holds the same per-PHROG alignments as A3M files (a3m/phrog_<n>.a3m), for searching PHROGs with HH-suite or MMseqs2. The upstream alignments already mark insert columns in lowercase; the A3M files keep those states and only drop the gap padding in insert columns. phu itself does not read this file.

ECOD (Evolutionary Classification of protein Domains) publishes no HMMs or alignments. The bundle has one model per F-group (family), named by its id (2004.1.1.5; phu screen reports it as ecod:2004.1.1.5), built with default hmmbuild settings from a FAMSA alignment of the family's F70 representatives (ECOD's domains clustered at 70% identity), from experimental and predicted structures alike. Domains classified only to the T level are left out. ecod/msa_a3m.tar.gz holds those alignments as a3m/<f_id>.a3m, with the model's own match columns. sequences.fa holds the 691,203 member sequences with ECOD's headers (uid|ecod_domain_id|f_id); families.tsv gives each family's F, T, H and X ids and names, architecture, Pfam accessions and member counts; domains.tsv gives each member's source (pdb, afdb, epp or uniparc) and accession. The ECOD sequences come from a Zenodo mirror (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24291646) of ECOD's own release files; cite ECOD: Schaeffer RD, et al. Nucleic Acids Res. 2025, doi:10.1093/nar/gkae1029.

The bundle's own manifest, phu-db.json, lists every upstream URL, SHA-256, byte size, license and record count, and the exact preparation steps that turn each upstream download into the installed file.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Each run writes the database provenance into the .phu/ folder of its output folder: the bundle version, the tarball SHA-256 and each database's upstream release. avger, screen --all-cazymes and screen --all-puls write it to .phu/run.json; other screen queries that name Pfam, KOfam or dbCAN models write it to .phu/query.json, with the SHA-256 of each database file used. Keep these files with your results.

docs.title: Citation
docs.text:
Cite the bundle version you used:

García-Botero C. Phu Databases, version phu-db-0.4.0. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19503347

Also cite the upstream databases your analysis relied on, following each project's own citation guidance:

  • Pfam: Mistry J, et al. Nucleic Acids Res. 2021;49(D1):D412–D419.
  • ECOD: Schaeffer RD, et al. Nucleic Acids Res. 2025. doi:10.1093/nar/gkae1029.
  • PHROGs: Terzian P, et al. NAR Genom. Bioinform. 2021;3(3):lqab067.
  • KOfam, dbCAN and CheckAMG: see their project pages.

docs.title: Upgrading from PHU 0.9.x and earlier
docs.text:
Earlier releases downloaded each database separately and managed them with phu dbs. phu dbs prepare remains and now installs the single bundle. The list, status, refresh and remove subcommands are gone; they only print a notice pointing to phu dbs prepare.

PHU no longer reads the old per-database folders in PHU_DB_FOLDER (pfam/, kofam/, dbcan/, avg/ and vscore/) and never deletes them. Once the bundle is installed you can remove them yourself to free about 10 GB; the bundle lives in phu-db/ beside them.

docs.title: Screen thresholds
docs.text:
This page is the reference for how phu screen decides which hits count and which contigs are kept. For a task-oriented overview, see the screen guide.

These are acceptance rules for profile hits. They do not prove that a contig is viral or that a gene is an auxiliary viral gene; for that, see the avger scientific interpretation.

docs.title: The decision in brief
docs.text:
For every hit pyHMMER reports as included:

  1. Apply the rule of the model's kind (table below).
  2. Apply --min-protein-coverage, if set.
  3. Compare the hit's score with the effective minimum bit score.
  4. Keep the hit only if its E-value is at most --max-evalue (default 1e-6).

Contigs with at least one remaining hit are then kept or dropped by --combine-mode (see Combining hits into contigs).

Model kind Rule Turn it off with Your own HMM Aligns to more than 0.35 of the model --min-hmm-coverage 0 Pfam Pfam's gathering (GA) cutoff, applied during the search --no-cut-ga KOfam The KO's threshold from ko_list, on the KO's score type --no-use-kofam-thresholds PHROG At least 60 bits, and at least 0.5 of model and of protein aligned --no-use-phrog-thresholds ECOD At least 0.5 of the model aligned --no-use-ecod-thresholds dbCAN Domain (independent) E-value below 1e-15 and more than 0.35 of the model aligned always on

A hit without a usable alignment fails any rule that needs coverage.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
Coverage counts every reported domain of a hit, with overlapping domains counted once, on the model side (hmm_coverage) and on the protein side (protein_coverage). This is how phu avger and CheckAMG compute it. Both values are written to the result tables.

--min-protein-coverage F is off by default. When set, a hit passes only if its domains cover at least the fraction F of the protein, for every kind of model and in addition to that kind's rule.

docs.title: Your own HMMs
docs.text: A hit to one of your HMMs must align to more than --min-hmm-coverage of the model (default 0.35; 0 turns the filter off). This removes matches to a small piece of the family. The filter does not apply to database models, which have their own rules. An HMM file of yours is treated as your own even if its name looks like a database id.

docs.title: Pfam
docs.text:
Pfam accessions are resolved to the bundle's Pfam models. With --cut-ga (the default), pyHMMER applies each model's curated gathering cutoff during the search. With --no-cut-ga, only --min-bitscore and --max-evalue apply.

Gathering cutoffs exist only in Pfam models. In a run that mixes Pfam with other models (your own, KOfam, PHROG, ECOD, dbCAN), the Pfam models are searched with their cutoffs and the others without.

docs.title: KOfam
docs.text:
KOfam models come with a threshold and a score type (full or domain) for each KO, from KOfam's ko_list. With --use-kofam-thresholds (the default):

  • the score compared is the full-sequence score, or the best domain's score when the KO's score type is domain;
  • the minimum is the KO's threshold, or --min-bitscore if that is higher.

So --min-bitscore can only make KOfam stricter. The E-value test always uses the full-sequence E-value, even for KOs scored by domain.

For example, a KO with threshold 136.43 and score type full rejects hits scoring 15 to 20 bits, however good their domain scores look in the domain table.

docs.title: PHROG
docs.text: PHROG models have no curated cutoffs. A hit must score at least 60 bits and align to at least 0.5 of the model and 0.5 of the protein, the rule phu avger uses.

docs.title: ECOD
docs.text: ECOD models have no curated cutoffs either. They describe single domains, often within longer proteins, so a hit must align to at least 0.5 of the model but may cover any part of the protein. Only the E-value applies with --no-use-ecod-thresholds.

docs.title: dbCAN
docs.text:
A dbCAN hit must have a best-domain independent E-value below 1e-15 and align to more than 0.35 of the model, the cutoffs dbCAN recommends for its HMMs. These rules are always on.

With --all-cazymes, every CAZyme family is searched once and any family hit keeps its contig. With --all-puls, a PUL matches a contig when all its families hit there, and a contig is kept when at least one PUL matches. PULs that name families missing from the installed dbCAN models are skipped and listed in .phu/run.json.

docs.title: Bit score and E-value
docs.text:
Each hit has a full-sequence bit score and the score of its best domain. The full-sequence score is used, except for KOs scored by domain (see KOfam).

--min-bitscore, if set, applies to every model. --max-evalue applies to the hit's full-sequence E-value, never to the per-domain E-values in the domain table.

docs.title: Combining hits into contigs
docs.text:
After filtering, contigs are kept by --combine-mode:

  • any: at least one query hits the contig.
  • all: every query hits the contig.
  • threshold: at least --min-hmm-hits different queries hit the contig.

Each ecod: id is one query, met by a hit to any of its families. For each kept contig, the best hits of each matched query are reported, up to --top-per-contig (default 1).

docs.title: Domain tables
docs.text: --keep-domtbl (the default) keeps hmmsearch's per-domain table of each model (<model>-hmmsearch-domains.tbl). The decisions above are made from pyHMMER's results directly, not by reading these files back; keep them to audit why a hit passed or failed.

docs.title: Missing external executable
docs.text:
cluster requires the external vclust executable; it is the only external program PHU runs. Confirm that it is available on PATH:

command -v vclust

Install the missing program using the environment or package manager appropriate for your system, then rerun the command. PHU does not install every external binary automatically.

docs.title: Database install fails
docs.text:
Databases install automatically on first use, or with phu dbs prepare; see Databases and Provenance. Common causes of a failed install:

  • Not enough disk space. The install needs about 20 GB free in PHU_DB_FOLDER and reports the exact amount when it stops.
  • No internet access on the node. Download the bundle elsewhere and set PHU_DB_BUNDLE to its path.

  • Checksum mismatch. The download or the PHU_DB_BUNDLE file is corrupt or is a different bundle version. Download the version named in the error.

  • Certificate errors (CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED). Some Python installs have no certificate bundle. Point Python at the system one, for example export SSL_CERT_FILE=/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt.

  • A slow or stalled download. The download shows its progress and resumes where it stopped when you run the command again. It fetches 8 parts of the bundle at once; if your network or proxy objects to that, set PHU_DB_CONNECTIONS=1.

An interrupted install leaves nothing half-installed; run the command again. If you suspect an installed file was changed, run phu dbs prepare --verify (or any command once with PHU_DB_VERIFY=1): it re-hashes every database file and reinstalls if a check fails.

A database folder you cannot write to, such as an install shared by a colleague, works as is: PHU keeps the index files it builds in your own cache folder. See Databases and Provenance.

docs.title: Cache or permissions errors
docs.text:
Set a writable cache location explicitly when the default home cache is not available:

PHU_CACHE_DIR="$PWD/.phu-cache" phu --version

Use PHU_CACHE=off for a diagnostic run without cache reuse. phu clean --cache removes the resolved cache directory, so verify PHU_CACHE_DIR before using it.

docs.title: Input and empty results
docs.text: Check FASTA headers and sequences when a run fails during parsing. A valid FASTA must contain headers beginning with > and nucleotide or protein sequence text appropriate to the command. No hits is a valid scientific result and is reported differently from an execution error; inspect the command's stderr and exit status before treating an empty result as a failure.

docs.title: Interrupted runs and stale outputs
docs.text: Use a new output directory for a clean diagnostic run. Review existing files before rerunning into a directory that contains results. PHU's commands do not provide one uniform overwrite contract across all workflows; do not assume that stale files are removed automatically.

docs.title: Debug diagnostics
docs.text: The workflow commands (screen, jack, cluster, avger, normalize-lineage, simplify-taxa) accept --verbose and --quiet. Preserve the complete command, version, input identifiers, database status, and error output when reporting a reproducible problem.

docs.title: Run logs
docs.text:
When the output is not a terminal (for example a SLURM .out file), each step prints one line when it starts and one when it ends, with the wall-clock time and the step's real duration, and without colour codes:

[14:02:11] Predicting proteins ...
[14:04:25] Predicting proteins done in 2m14s
[14:04:25] Running HMM searches ...
[14:09:02] Running HMM searches failed after 4m37s: <error message>

A step ends with done in, failed after, skipped after, or cancelled after. On a terminal the same steps are shown as live lines with a running timer.

--verbose adds one line per tool invocation, always prefixed with [cmd]. External programs (vclust) are shown as the exact, shell-quoted command that was executed, including any output redirection. In-process steps (pyrodigal-gv gene prediction, pyhmmer hmmsearch and jackhmmer, pyfamsa alignment, pytrimal trimming, sequence extraction) are shown as the function name followed by the key=value parameters that determine the result:

[cmd] pyrodigal_gv.ViralGeneFinder contigs=4 mode=meta meta=True min_gene=90 max_overlap=89 translation_table=auto training_table=none min_protein_len_aa=30 threads=2
[cmd] pyhmmer.hmmsearch hmm_files=1 models=1 sequences=19 cpus=2 parallel=queries bit_cutoffs=gathering hmm_mode=pure ...
[cmd] phu.extract_records input=contigs.fna ids=3 outputs=1

Extract them with grep '^\[cmd\]' run.log. Gene prediction prints no [cmd] line when the predicted proteins come from the cache, because nothing is run. --quiet hides the step lines and the [cmd] lines; errors are still printed. Nothing is written to a log file: redirect stdout and stderr to keep a record.

docs.title: avger
docs.text:
phu avger predicts proteins from trusted viral contigs and annotates them against the complete Pfam, KOfam and PHROG databases, then applies the provisional AVG candidate and curation workflow. It writes deterministic TSV tables for all genes, candidates, predictions, and supporting evidence.

This is the supported annotation/evidence workflow. The repository also contains the implementation modules used internally by this command; they are not exposed as separate subcommands.

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text: phu avger -i contigs.fa -o phu-avger

Candidate scoring uses the AVG reference database's V-score and VL-score tables.

docs.title: PHROG
docs.text:
PHROG (Terzian et al., 2021) groups the proteins of prokaryotic viruses into families. Many phage proteins have no Pfam or KOfam match, so PHROG gives avger evidence for genes the other two databases leave blank. It is searched by default; --no-phrog skips it, which saves the largest of the three searches.

PHROG takes part in every step, the same way Pfam and KOfam do:

  • Scoring. The best PHROG hit of each protein at E-value 1e-5 supplies its V-score and VL-score, and the contig's PHROG AVL is their average.
  • Candidates. A gene is a candidate when the candidate rule holds in at least one of the three databases.
  • Annotation. PHROG has no curated per-model cutoffs. A PHROG annotation is reported, and used for classification, when the hit scores at least 60 bits (CheckAMG's cutoff) and passes the coverage rule, which applies to every database (see Outputs).
  • Classification. The reference tables list PHROGs that support the physiology (putative_apg) and regulatory (putative_areg) classes. They list none for putative_amg, so PHROG alone never makes an AMG call.
  • Filters. The filter lists name PHROGs of core viral functions, such as integrases and major head proteins. A strict PHROG hit to one of them blocks the class, exactly as a Pfam or KOfam filter match does. A gene that Pfam or KOfam would classify can therefore be filtered because its PHROG hit says it is a structural or replication protein.

The PHROG models are HMMER models built for the phu database bundle from the official PHROG alignments (see Databases and Provenance). The phrog_model_coverage and phrog_protein_coverage columns are the fractions of the model and of the protein that the hit's domains cover.

Coverage rule. Every strict hit, whatever its database, must align over at least 50% of both the model and the protein (--min-coverage; 0 turns it off). Coverage is computed as CheckAMG computes it: every reported domain of the hit counts, and overlapping domains are counted once. CheckAMG applies the same rule with a default of 40%. The relaxed scoring track never uses coverage.

docs.title: What AVG means
docs.text:
AVG means auxiliary viral gene: a viral gene that is auxiliary to core viral functions. The broader AVG category includes genes that may increase viral fitness by maintaining or manipulating host functions during infection. In this project, the proposed classes are:

  • AMG (auxiliary metabolic gene): associated with maintaining or manipulating host metabolism during infection.
  • APG (auxiliary physiology gene): associated with a host physiology-related function.
  • AReG (auxiliary regulatory gene): associated with regulating host gene expression or other cellular regulatory processes.

These classes are written as putative_amg, putative_apg, and putative_areg in the output tables. They are proposed functional classes, not confirmed biological categories. Candidate effects may be small or large and condition-dependent, and a class assignment requires evidence beyond function prediction.

This terminology follows Martin et al. (2025). The avger workflow uses viral-context evidence, profile annotations, V/VL scores, AVL, and curated reference records to prioritize AVG candidates. An AVG is not synonymous with an AMG: AMGs are one functional subset, while the broader AVG framework also includes non-metabolic effects on bacterial-host fitness. These computational signals do not by themselves demonstrate a fitness effect in a bacterial host.

This interpretation is consistent with the broader view that virus-host relationships involve both host-range effects and molecular interactions between viral and host proteins. Iuchi et al. provide a review of those bioinformatics approaches, including their limitations and dataset biases; they do not define this project's AVG classes or score cutoffs. Therefore, avger results are computational evidence for prioritization and require biological validation.

docs.title: Literature context and provenance
docs.text:
The workflow combines established tools and databases with a project-specific decision layer:

  • Gene prediction: Prodigal and its Python interface, Pyrodigal, provide the coding-sequence prediction step. Unless explicitly provided, the translation table is selected by each contig's pyrodigal-gv model. The selected --mode, --ttable, and length filters affect which proteins enter downstream annotation.
  • Profile annotation: HMMER, accessed through PyHMMER, supplies profile-HMM searches. Pfam model cutoffs, KOfam's KO-specific thresholds and fixed PHROG score and coverage cutoffs are used as annotation criteria; a passing profile match is not, by itself, evidence of an AVG.
  • Viral-family evidence: V-Score-Search motivates the use of family-level V and VL scores and genome/scaffold averages. Its AV/AVL thresholds are designed for viral-sequence identification and must not be repurposed as universal protein-level AVG probabilities.
  • Input quality: CheckV-style completeness and quality assessment belong to the upstream viral-sequence assessment. avger expects trusted viral contigs and does not replace that assessment.
  • AVG decision layer: the database-specific AVL calculation, strict candidate predicate, AMG weights, class filters, and final statuses are the provisional rules implemented by this project. They should be reported with their parameters and reference-database manifest, rather than presented as conclusions established by the cited tool papers.

docs.title: AMG weight
docs.text:
The amg_weight is a confidence or support value supplied by the positive AMG reference table; it is not a V-score, VL-score, or probability that a gene is an AVG. For each candidate, avger considers the matching positive AMG records and uses their maximum available weight. By default, an AMG record must have a weight of at least 0.6, configured with --min-amg-weight, to support the putative_amg class. APG and AReG evidence is not filtered by this AMG weight.

If AMG evidence is present but all of its weights are below the threshold, the candidate receives the below_amg_weight status unless another supported class survives. The weight threshold is a project/reference-database curation rule, not a universal biological cutoff.

docs.title: Class filters
docs.text:
The --filter-mode option controls class-specific negative evidence from the reference database:

Mode Behavior standard Enforces only filter_essential; other matches are warnings. strict Enforces all configured filter categories. none Records filter evidence but does not remove a class.

This separation follows the broader virus-host interaction literature: sequence or protein-level computational signals can prioritize hypotheses, but they do not demonstrate a host benefit or a physical virus-host interaction without experimental or ecological validation (Iuchi et al., 2023).

avger separates three kinds of evidence:

  1. Annotation evidence: a predicted protein has a Pfam, KOfam or PHROG profile match that passes the database-specific score threshold and independent E-value cutoff (1e-5 by default).
  2. Viral-family evidence: the matched protein family has a V-score in the V-Score-Search table. Higher V-scores indicate stronger virus association for the family; they are not proof that every individual protein is viral.
  3. AVG interpretation: the protein is an auxiliary viral gene candidate only when its annotation is evaluated in viral sequence context and a curated internal rule supports that interpretation. A metabolic or host-like function alone is not sufficient evidence of an AVG.

The V-Score-Search workflow recommends predicting ORFs with pyrodigal-gv, searching Pfam and KEGG/KOfam profiles at maximum E-value 1e-5, and using genome-level average V-scores (AV-scores) and average Vᴸ-scores (AVᴸ-scores) with fragment-size-specific cutoffs for viral sequence identification. It also recommends filtering candidate viral sequences using CheckV completeness. These are viral-classification criteria, not AVG-classification criteria. avger does not silently apply them to individual proteins; the input contigs should therefore already have a documented viral-sequence assessment.

Thus, a candidate (a true in the rule_avg_candidate column) is an AVG candidate record, not a confirmed AVG call. A named classification requires an internal AVG rule that combines the relevant KOfam/Pfam evidence, V-score support where appropriate, and the already- established viral context. Passing a viral AV/AVᴸ cutoff does not by itself make a gene an AVG.

docs.title: Evidence levels
docs.text:
Output situation Scientific meaning Row in avg-predictions.tsv Candidate received a final curated AVG class Row in detailed/filtered-candidates.tsv Candidate passed the AVL/V/VL predicate, but no final class was assigned or classes conflicted Row in detailed/gene-annotations.tsv Predicted gene, including strict annotation fields and any scoring evidence

V-scores should not be treated as universal protein-level probability cutoffs. Their interpretation depends on the database family and the V-Score-Search methodology. See the V-Score-Search documentation and Zhou et al., V-Score-Search (preprint, doi:10.1101/2024.10.24.619987).

docs.title: Threshold boundary
docs.text:
The published Table 1 AV-score and AVᴸ-score cutoffs belong to the upstream viral-sequence classification step (Phase 4). They answer:

Is this genome or fragment sufficiently virus-like?

AVG classification is a separate downstream step (Phase 5). It answers:

Given a viral sequence, does this particular gene have evidence consistent with an auxiliary viral function?

Therefore, the Table 1 values must not be used as per-protein AVG thresholds.

docs.title: AVG candidate criteria
docs.text:
For each contig and database independently, avger uses the relaxed-track best significant hits and calculates:

$$ AVL_{db} = \frac{\sum VL\text{-scores of proteins with significant best hits in } db} {\text{number of proteins with significant best hits in } db} $$

The denominator is the number of scored significant hits in that database, not the total number of predicted proteins. Evidence from one database is never combined with the contig score of another.

A database-specific candidate requires all three strict inequalities:

  • gene Vᴸ-score < 3;
  • gene V-score < 10;
  • same-database contig AVL-score > 3.

rule_pfam_candidate, rule_kofam_candidate and rule_phrog_candidate are evaluated independently. The combined rule_avg_candidate is true when any database-specific candidate is true. The cutoffs are configurable with --scaffold-avl-cutoff, --gene-vl-cutoff, and --gene-v-cutoff; their defaults are 3, 3, and 10. Boundary values are excluded.

flowchart TD
    A[Trusted viral contigs] --> B[Predict proteins]
    B --> C[Annotate against Pfam, KOfam and PHROG]
    C --> D[Relaxed and strict annotation tracks]
    D --> E[Average relaxed VL-scores per contig and database]
    E --> F{AVL > cutoff and gene VL < cutoff and gene V < cutoff?}
    F -->|No| G[Not a Zhou candidate]
    F -->|Yes| H[rule_avg_candidate]
    H --> I[Match positive AVG reference evidence]
    I --> J[Apply AMG weight threshold]
    J --> K[Apply standard, strict, or no class filters]
    K --> L{Final named class?}
    L -->|No| M[Candidate without final classification]
    L -->|Yes| N[avg-predictions.tsv]
    G --> O[detailed/gene-annotations.tsv]
    M --> O
    O --> P[detailed/avg-evidence.tsv]
    O --> Q[Metadata: .phu/run.json]

The Pfam, KOfam and PHROG branches represented by this flow are independent; their AVL values are never mixed. AVL is therefore an active candidate-selection criterion, not merely a reported summary value.

docs.title: Flank evidence
docs.text: The current registered avger command does not apply flank-support criteria. Its context evidence comes from the reference tables, AMG weighting, and class filters described below.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Start with output-info.txt: it is written by every run and holds the run's counts, what each file is, and a data dictionary for every column of avg-predictions.tsv.

At the top level:

  • avg-predictions.tsv: the main result. One row per predicted auxiliary viral gene, with its class, the function and reference entries that support it, the rule values that made it a candidate, and its best strict hit per database.
  • contig-summary.tsv: one row per contig, with gene counts, the AVL of each database, and candidate and prediction counts by class.
  • avg-proteins.faa: amino-acid sequences of the predicted genes; each header carries the class and function.
  • output-info.txt: counts, file notes and the data dictionary.

Under detailed/:

  • gene-annotations.tsv: one row per predicted gene, including annotation, V/VL scoring, AVL, candidate, curation, and classification fields. Each database has its own group of columns (pfam_*, kofam_*, phrog_*); the phrog_* columns are always present and are empty when PHROG was not searched. Empty scoring fields mean that no matching AVG reference record was available; they can prevent a gene from becoming a candidate.
  • filtered-candidates.tsv: candidates that did not become predictions, one row per gene, with the status and reason (no supported class, below the AMG weight, filtered, or a class conflict).
  • avg-evidence.tsv: audit records from relaxed/strict hits and reference matches.
  • hmm-hits-relaxed.tsv.gz and hmm-hits-strict.tsv.gz: all annotation hits when --keep-hits is supplied.

And .phu/run.json: automatically generated provenance metadata containing parameters, database manifests, cache information, schema version, output counts, and timestamps. It is not needed to read the TSV results, but should be retained when runs need to be reproduced, compared, or audited.

The Pfam, KOfam, PHROG and AVG databases install automatically on the first run (see Databases and Provenance):

phu avger -i contigs.fa -o phu-avger

The AVG reference database supplies the V-score/VL-score tables, positive evidence, and class filters used by the run.

The prediction cache is shared with screen and jack. Its key includes the input contigs and prediction settings (--mode, --ttable, and the relevant length filters), but not annotation settings. A successful run prints whether the prediction cache was hit and the paths to the generated output files.

docs.title: Classifications
docs.text:
Classifications use the versioned rules in the prepared AVG reference database. The final status is classified, not_candidate, filtered, below_amg_weight, class_conflict, or unclassified_candidate. The selected class is written to avg_class; the evidence and manifest preserve the inputs and provenance.

When no named class survives the weight and filter steps, the result is unclassified_candidate; it must not be interpreted as a confirmed AVG.

docs.title: Scientific basis and attribution
docs.text:
phu avger applies the V-score, VL-score, and scaffold AVL-score framework introduced by Zhou et al. to identify candidate auxiliary viral genes. These scores describe protein-family and viral-context evidence; the database-specific candidate predicates are adapted from that framework and remain candidate rules, not experimental validation.

Functional classification and post-candidate curation use versioned reference tables developed by CheckAMG and the Anantharaman Lab, including AMG, APG, and AReG positive lists, precomputed AMG_weight values, and class-specific filters. AMG_weight is reference-level metadata, not a probability calculated from the query sequence. phu normalizes and indexes selected upstream records for local use; it does not create or reproduce the complete CheckAMG workflow.

Interpretation and reporting follow the cautionary principles outlined by Martin et al. Results are therefore reported as putative, annotation-supported or reference-supported predictions. A classified result means exactly one putative class remains after configured reference-based curation; it does not mean experimentally validated. Sequence detection, annotation, viral context, expression, biochemical activity, host effects, and viral fitness are distinct claims. Functional annotation or a filter match does not establish biological activity, altered metabolic flux, or physiological effect, and absence from a positive list does not disprove auxiliary function. Stronger evidence could include viral genomic context, phylogeny, infection-time expression, biochemical characterization, or infection experiments.

Together, Zhou et al. provide candidate detection, CheckAMG provides curated functional evidence, and Martin et al. provide interpretive caution. phu provides the lightweight, traceable integration and reporting layer.

docs.title: How to cite this analysis
docs.text: Please cite Zhou K. et al., V- and VL-scores unveil viral signatures and origins of protein families, Nature Communications (2026), DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-72028-0, the CheckAMG v1.1.1 data release recorded in .phu/run.json and the Anantharaman Lab repository, Martin et al. (2025), and phu itself. Cite Pfam, KOfamKOALA, PyHMMER, and pyrodigal-gv as applicable. The CheckAMG release currently supplies software and data attribution rather than an official peer-reviewed paper citation.

docs.title: cluster
docs.text: Sequence clustering wrapper around the external vclust tool, with four preconfigured modes for common viral genomics workflows. Each mode follows one of vclust's documented use cases; --vclust-params adjusts them.

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text: phu cluster --mode <MODE> --input-contigs <FASTA_FILE> [OPTIONS]

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
• dereplication — remove redundant sequences, keeping one representative per group (greedy CD-HIT-like clustering on ANI and coverage).
  • votu — viral Operational Taxonomic Units with MIUViG thresholds (Leiden clustering on ANI ≥ 95% and query coverage ≥ 85%).
  • genus — genus-level groups of complete genomes: complete linkage on total ANI (tANI) ≥ 70%.
  • species — species-level groups of complete genomes: complete linkage on tANI ≥ 95%.

genus and species follow vclust's VIRIDIC-like recipe ("Classify viruses into species and genera"), which uses the 70% and 95% genome-wide identity thresholds applied to bacteriophages.

phu cluster --mode genus -i genomes.fna -o phu-genus
phu cluster --mode species -i genomes.fna -o phu-species

docs.text:

The align output filter of dereplication and votu always equals their clustering thresholds, so it only shrinks the ANI table and never removes a pair the clustering would use.

docs.title: ANI, tANI and the clustering algorithm
docs.text:
• ANI is the identity of the aligned regions only. Two genomes that share one short, nearly identical region have a high ANI, so ANI modes also require a query coverage (the aligned fraction of the query sequence).
  • tANI (total ANI) counts identical bases over the full length of both genomes, so unaligned sequence lowers it; it combines identity and coverage in one number, as VIRIDIC does. A genome sharing 80% of its length with another at 99.6% identity has an ANI near 0.99 but a tANI near 0.80: same genus, different species.
  • Complete linkage (genus, species) puts two genomes in the same group only when every pair in the group passes the threshold. Single linkage would chain genomes that are each similar to a neighbour but not to each other; Leiden (votu) and CD-HIT (dereplication) are graph and greedy-representative methods suited to large sets of contigs.

docs.title: Use with complete genomes
docs.text: Genus and species groups are operational: they are numerical clusters, not ICTV taxa, and phu does not assign taxon names. Use them with complete or near-complete genomes. tANI is computed over each sequence's full length, so a fragment of a genome has a low tANI to the complete genome it came from and can end up in its own genus or species group. For metagenomic contigs of mixed completeness, use votu (ANI with a coverage requirement) instead, and treat genus and species groups of incomplete sequences as provisional.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
phu-genus/
├── prefilter-pairs.txt             # vclust prefilter: sequence pairs worth aligning
├── ani-pairs.tsv                   # vclust align: ANI, tANI and coverage per sequence pair
├── ani-sequence-ids.tsv            # vclust align: sequence IDs and lengths used by clustering
├── genus-clusters.tsv              # cluster assignments (see the table above for each mode)
├── cluster-representative-ids.txt  # one representative ID per input sequence's cluster
└── cluster-representatives.fna     # representative sequences

Each cluster's representative is its longest sequence (vclust --out-repr).

docs.title: Advanced: custom vclust parameters
docs.text:
--vclust-params takes vclust flags as one quoted string and passes each to its step (prefilter, align or cluster). Settings are resolved in this order, later ones winning: the mode's defaults, then --vclust-params. A flag given there replaces the default instead of being added a second time.

# Stricter genus groups
phu cluster --mode genus -i genomes.fna --vclust-params="--tani 0.75"

# vOTUs at 97% ANI; the align filter follows the new threshold
phu cluster --mode votu -i contigs.fna --vclust-params="--ani 0.97"

# Larger datasets: analyse 20% of k-mers and write a compact ANI table
phu cluster --mode votu -i contigs.fna --vclust-params="--kmers-fraction 0.2 --outfmt lite"

phu stops before running vclust when the parameters contradict each other:

Combination Why it is rejected An align filter above the clustering threshold of the same measure, e.g. --mode genus with --out-ani 0.95 Removes pairs the clustering needs. --metric without that metric's threshold, e.g. --mode genus with --metric ani A tANI threshold would otherwise be read as an ANI one, or none used. A threshold below the mode's prefilter identity without --min-ident, e.g. --mode votu with --ani 0.90 The prefilter at 0.95 would drop pairs before alignment; add --min-ident 0.9.

docs.title: Single-character sequence names
docs.text: vclust 1.3.1 align --filter on two or more threads skips genome pairs whose sequence names are a single character (>A, >x). When the input has such a name, phu runs the alignment step on one thread and says so; the other steps keep --threads. Rename the sequences to align in parallel.

docs.title: What does it do?
docs.text:
The phu jack command iteratively screens contigs from one or more seed protein markers using pyhmmer.hmmer.jackhmmer. It predicts proteins from the input contigs, searches them against each seed, and uses successive iterations to expand the detected protein family.

This command is useful when a trusted marker protein is available but a profile HMM is not. Interpret expanded hits as sequence-similarity evidence, not as a validated functional or taxonomic assignment.

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
phu jack -i <INPUT_CONTIGS> [OPTIONS] [<SEED_MARKER>] [--phrog QUERY ...]

<SEED_MARKER> is a protein FASTA file and may contain one or more seed sequences. PHROG families can be seeds too, with --phrog (see PHROG seeds); give a FASTA, --phrog, or both.

Examples:

phu jack -i contigs.fa marker_seed.faa
phu jack -i contigs.fa --combine-mode all marker_seeds.faa
phu jack -i contigs.fa --iterations 7 --inc-evalue 1e-4 marker_seed.faa
phu jack -i contigs.fa --phrog alias:portal
phu jack -i contigs.fa --combine-mode all --phrog phrog_2 marker_seed.faa

docs.title: Iterative search
docs.text:
Each seed is searched independently with jackhmmer. The --iterations option sets the maximum number of iterations, while --inc-evalue controls which hits are included in the next iteration. Final hits are filtered by --max-evalue. The --top-per-contig option limits retained hits by bitscore after filtering.

When multiple seed sequences are provided, --combine-mode controls contig retention:

  • any: retain contigs hit by at least one seed.
  • all: retain contigs hit by every seed.
  • threshold: retain contigs hit by at least --min-seed-hits seeds.

docs.title: PHROG seeds
docs.text:
--phrog QUERY (repeatable) uses PHROG families as seeds. Queries are those of phu phrogs resolve: phrog_<n>, alias:<name>, category:<name> or 'annot:<annotation>'. Use phu phrogs resolve first to see what a query selects.

  • How a PHROG seed is searched. The first iteration searches with the PHROG model itself, a profile built from the whole family; later iterations use models rebuilt from the included hits, as for sequence seeds. --iterations, --inc-evalue and --max-evalue apply to both. --iterations 1 is a plain search with the PHROG model, the same search as phu screen phrog_<n> but with jack's thresholds. When nothing is included, the seed stops after one iteration, reported as converged, as jackhmmer does for a sequence seed.
  • Drift. Models rebuilt from hits can move away from the PHROG family, especially when the first iteration includes few or distant proteins. Check jackhmmer-iterations.tsv, and lower --iterations if later iterations add unexpected hits.
  • Cap. Each PHROG is one iterative search, and an alias or category can select dozens to thousands of PHROGs (alias:terl 54, category:tail 1,238). jack stops before predicting proteins when the selection is larger than --max-phrog-seeds (default 50). Narrow the query or raise the cap.
  • Seed groups. --combine-mode counts seed groups, not single seeds. Each FASTA sequence is a group, and each --phrog query is one group however many PHROGs it selects: the 54 PHROGs of alias:terl are alternatives for one marker. So --combine-mode all --phrog alias:terl --phrog alias:portal keeps contigs with a terminase and a portal hit, and --min-seed-hits 2 needs two different queries. A PHROG selected by two queries belongs to the first. Within a group, a protein hit by several PHROGs is kept once, by its best hit.
  • Mixing. FASTA and PHROG seeds can be combined. A FASTA record named like a selected PHROG (phrog_2) is refused, so that every seed ID is unique.
  • What a query meant. With --verbose, jack logs each query with the PHROG identifiers it selected, then each PHROG seed with its annotation, category and group (lines starting [cmd] phu.phrogs). The same is kept in .phu/query.json.

docs.title: Input and output
docs.text:
The input contigs are translated with pyrodigal using --mode, --min-gene-len, --min-protein-len-aa, and optionally --ttable. The resulting protein FASTA is cached and reused when the prediction inputs are unchanged. Use --keep-proteins to retain the FASTA in the output directory as predicted-proteins.faa (with the cache key in .phu/prediction.json).

A successful run writes these core outputs:

phu-jack/
├── matched-contigs.fna
├── matched-contig-ids.txt
├── jackhmmer-hits.tsv
└── jackhmmer-iterations.tsv

jackhmmer-hits.tsv contains final hit records and filtering metadata. jackhmmer-iterations.tsv records the per-iteration search summary. Both have a seed_source column (fasta or phrog) and a seed_group column (the FASTA seed ID, or the --phrog query that selected the PHROG). .phu/query.json records the seeds: the FASTA, the --phrog queries, and each PHROG seed with its annotation, category and the query that selected it, plus the database bundle's provenance. With --save-hmm, the final model is written as final-iteration.hmm for a single seed or under final-iteration-hmms/ for multiple seeds.

docs.text:
# Start with a trusted marker protein.
phu jack \
  --input-contigs viral_assembly.fasta \

docs.title: What does it do?
docs.text: The phu normalize-lineage command normalizes vContact lineage predictions into compact, rank-aware lineage values without renaming the input columns. It is intended for tables produced by vContact workflows.

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
phu normalize-lineage -i <INPUT_FILE> -o <OUTPUT_FILE> [OPTIONS]

The input delimiter is inferred from the filename unless --sep is supplied. The output table preserves the original columns and is written to the path provided by --output-file.

docs.title: Input and output
docs.text:
The command recognizes lineage prediction columns by their taxonomic rank, such as genus_prediction, family_prediction, and order_prediction. Missing values remain missing. Values that cannot be parsed are preserved rather than silently discarded.

For example:

novel_genus_1_of_Viruses
Viruses:NG1

Each novel_<rank>_<n> node becomes N plus the rank letter and its number (NR, NK, NP, NC, NO, NF, NSF, NG). The anchor comes first and the codes follow from the highest rank to the lowest.

docs.title: Unplaced ranks and the default anchor
docs.text:
vContact3 also writes unplaced_<rank> nodes, joined by _within_. They carry no number, so each one becomes U plus the same rank letter (UR, UK, UP, UC, UO, UF, USF, UG). The placeholder anchor default is written as DEF; any other anchor is kept as written.

Input Output unplaced_phylum_within_unplaced_kingdom_within_default DEF:UK:UP unplaced_class_within_unplaced_phylum_within_unplaced_kingdom_within_default DEF:UK:UP:UC unplaced_order_within_Caudoviricetes Caudoviricetes:UO novel_genus_1_of_novel_family_2_of_unplaced_order_within_Caudoviricetes Caudoviricetes:UO:NF2:NG1

A chain may mix novel_ and unplaced_ nodes, and either _of_ or _within_ may follow either kind of node. Every node must be of a strictly lower rank than the next one toward the anchor. A chain that breaks that order, has no anchor, or names an unknown rank is reported as unparsed and left as it was. Compact values that already use U codes are left unchanged, so running the command on its own output changes nothing.

The normalized values remain in their original columns. With --add-lineage, a compact lineage column is appended; without it, no new column is added.

docs.title: Normalization and quality checks
docs.text:
Existing compact values are left unchanged. The command reports the number of examined, normalized, unchanged, missing, unparsed, rank-mismatched, and multi-candidate cells in its QA summary.

The --strict option makes quality problems fatal: the command exits non-zero when values are unparsed or when a value's rank does not match its column. In non-strict mode, those values are retained and reported. Multiple candidates separated by || are normalized independently.

docs.title: phrogs
docs.text:
Find PHROG identifiers by alias, functional category or annotation, and pass them to phu screen, which accepts phrog_<n> identifiers as queries.

phu phrogs categories                 # categories and how many PHROGs each has
phu phrogs aliases                    # short names such as mcp, terl, portal
phu phrogs search "tail fiber"        # explore annotations
phu phrogs resolve alias:mcp category:lysis --ids-only

# Screen contigs for major capsid and terminase large subunit families
phu screen -i contigs.fna $(phu phrogs resolve alias:mcp alias:terl --ids-only)

# The same queries seed iterative searches in jack
phu jack -i contigs.fna --phrog alias:portal

Only the 38,880 PHROG families with a model (phrog_1 to phrog_38880) are listed, so every identifier printed can be searched. About 5,100 of them have a known function; the rest are in the category "unknown function". The PHROG annotation table also numbers entries above 38,880, almost all unannotated and without an alignment, apparently proteins that formed no family; they cannot be searched and phu phrogs leaves them out. The first use indexes the PHROG models, which takes a few minutes; phu screen phrog_<n> uses the same index.

docs.title: Queries for resolve
docs.text:
Query Selects phrog_216 one PHROG alias:mcp a curated group of annotations (see below) category:tail every PHROG of a functional category 'annot:portal protein' PHROGs whose annotation is exactly this text, ignoring letter case

Queries can be mixed; each PHROG is listed once, under the first query that selected it. A query that selects nothing stops with an explanation.

--ids-only prints the identifiers on one line for the shell; -o file.tsv also writes the table (phrog_id, annotation, category, query), a record of what each name meant in that run.

docs.title: Searching annotations
docs.text:
phu phrogs search is for exploring. It lists PHROGs whose annotation matches every word given, in any order, and is forgiving; the match column says how each row matched, and rows are ordered from the most literal match:

match Example query Finds exact large terminase, baseplat each word appears in the annotation alias:<name> mcp, TerL the annotations of that alias synonym:<term> capsid, MTase, RNR, ssb, psbA PHROG's wording for the term: head protein, methyltransferase, ribonucleotide reductase, single strand DNA binding, photosystem II D1 variant tail fibre, holins, tapemeasure, antirepressor British spelling, plurals, words written together or apart typo endolysine, intergrase a close spelling of a word of five letters or more

Synonyms are listed in phu/data/phrog_aliases.json and apply to search only. resolve stays literal, apart from category names, so that a run records exactly what was selected: explore with search, then select with resolve.

docs.title: Categories
docs.text:
PHROGs v4 has nine functional categories plus "unknown function": tail; head and packaging; connector; DNA, RNA and nucleotide metabolism; transcription regulation; lysis; integration and excision; moron, auxiliary metabolic gene and host takeover; other.

Category names are matched forgivingly, and phu says how it read the name:

You write Read as tail, TAIL, tails tail head, pack head and packaging dna DNA, RNA and nucleotide metabolism moron, amg, host takeover moron, auxiliary metabolic gene and host takeover lysys lysis

A name that fits several categories (category:a) is refused with the candidates listed.

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
Aliases are short names for groups of PHROG annotations, stored in phu/data/phrog_aliases.json. Each lists exact PHROG v4 annotation strings, so mcp selects "major head protein", "major capsid protein" and "major head and protease protein" but not "minor head protein". Run phu phrogs aliases for the current list and counts, and phu phrogs aliases --check to confirm every listed annotation still exists in the installed PHROG table.

Alias Annotations mcp major head protein; major capsid protein; major head and protease protein terl, ters terminase large / small subunit portal, scaffold, head-tail portal; head scaffolding; head-tail connector and adaptors neck, collar neck and tail-completion proteins; collar proteins tmp, tail-sheath, tail-tube, baseplate tail structure tail-fiber, tail-spike tail fibers (not assembly chaperones); tail spikes and receptor-binding tail proteins holin, endolysin, spanin lysis integrase, excisionase, anti-repressor integration and regulation

moron and amg are shortcuts for the category "moron, auxiliary metabolic gene and host takeover".

The aliases follow PHROG's own annotation wording; they are a convenience, not a classification. Annotation text describes a family's best-known member, so review hits before drawing functional conclusions.

docs.title: Source
docs.text: Terzian P, et al. PHROG: families of prokaryotic virus proteins clustered using remote homology. NAR Genom Bioinform. 2021;3(3):lqab067.

docs.title: screen
docs.text:
phu screen finds the contigs that carry the protein families you ask for. It predicts the proteins of your contigs, searches them with profile HMMs, and keeps the contigs whose proteins match.

Use it to pull viral contigs out of a metagenomic assembly by their marker proteins, to find contigs that carry a gene of interest, or to collect the proteins behind a family for a new model.

phu screen -i contigs.fa PF00589                  # one Pfam family
phu screen -i contigs.fa phrog_216 ecod:2004.1    # a PHROG and an ECOD homology group
phu screen -i contigs.fa my-models/*.hmm          # your own HMMs

The matching contigs are written to phu-screen/matched-contigs.fna.

Input

phu screen takes DNA contigs (FASTA). If you already have proteins, search them with pyHMMER or HMMER directly.

docs.title: What you can search for
docs.text:
Each query is one of your own HMM files or a family named from the phu databases. You can mix kinds in one run.

Query Example What it names When a hit counts Your HMM file capsid.hmm The model(s) in the file Aligns to more than 35% of the model (--min-hmm-coverage) Pfam PF00589, PF00589.17 A Pfam family Pfam's curated gathering cutoff (--cut-ga) KOfam K00001 A KEGG Orthology group The KO's own score threshold (--use-kofam-thresholds) PHROG phrog_216 A PHROG family (phrog_1 to phrog_38880) 60 bits, and half of both model and protein aligned (--use-phrog-thresholds) ECOD ecod:2004.1.1.5, ecod:2004.1 An ECOD family, or every family in a larger group Half of the model aligned (--use-ecod-thresholds) dbCAN family GH128, cbm89 A CAZyme family (case does not matter) Domain E-value below 1e-15 and more than 35% of the model aligned dbCAN PUL PUL0621 The CAZyme families of one PUL Every family found on the same contig

Every hit must also have an E-value of at most 1e-6 (--max-evalue). --min-protein-coverage 0.5, off by default, further requires every hit to cover half of its protein, whatever the model; this drops single domains found in long multi-domain proteins. The first query that names a database family installs the database bundle, if it is not installed yet (see Databases). The full rules are in Screen thresholds.

docs.title: Pfam and KOfam
docs.text: Pfam accessions may carry a version (PF00589.17 is read as PF00589). Pfam models keep their curated gathering (GA) cutoffs, also when queried together with other kinds of model; --no-cut-ga turns them off and leaves only --max-evalue and --min-bitscore. KOfam models use the per-KO threshold and score type (full sequence or domain) from KOfam's ko_list; --no-use-kofam-thresholds turns them off.

docs.title: PHROG
docs.text:
PHROGs are phage protein families. PHROG has no curated per-model cutoffs, so a hit must score at least 60 bits and align to at least half of both the model and the protein, the rule phu avger uses. --no-use-phrog-thresholds drops that rule. The function and category of each queried PHROG are printed and recorded in .phu/query.json.

To pick PHROGs by name or category instead of number, use phu phrogs:

phu screen -i contigs.fa $(phu phrogs resolve alias:mcp alias:terl --ids-only)

docs.title: ECOD
docs.text:
ECOD classifies protein domains by evolutionary relationship, at four levels. You can query any of them with ecod: and a dotted id:

Level Example Meaning F (family) ecod:2004.1.1.5 One family: one model T (topology) ecod:2004.1.1 Every family with this fold topology H (homology) ecod:2004.1 Every family thought to share an ancestor X (possible homology) ecod:2004 Every family in the broadest group

The bundle has one model per F-group, 32,041 in ECOD v295.2, built from ECOD's representative domains. Group and family names are in families.tsv of the installed ecod database, and hits name their model as ecod:<family id>.

ECOD models describe single domains, often within longer proteins, so a hit must align to at least half of the model but may cover any part of the protein. --no-use-ecod-thresholds drops that rule. .phu/query.json records what each ecod: id expanded to, and the names and Pfam accessions of every family searched.

Broad groups search many models

ecod:2004.1, the P-loop homology group, expands to 556 families. Expect one domain table per family in the output folder; turn them off with --no-keep-domtbl.

docs.title: dbCAN families and PULs
docs.text:
dbCAN family names are matched against the installed dbCAN models, whatever their case. A PUL id expands to the CAZyme families of that PUL (from dbCAN-PUL's cazymes_predicted_dbcan), and by default every family must be found on the same contig; use --combine-mode threshold to accept part of the signature. Only one PUL can be queried per run, and not together with other queries. To search all CAZymes or all PULs at once, see CAZymes and PULs.

A PUL match means its CAZyme families occur together on a contig. It does not show that the contig carries that PUL or predict its substrate.

docs.title: Combining queries
docs.text:
With several queries, --combine-mode decides which contigs are kept:

Mode Keeps a contig when Use it for any (default) At least one query hits Collecting everything related to any query all Every query hits Requiring a set of markers together threshold At least --min-hmm-hits queries hit Requiring, for example, 3 of 5 markers

Each ecod: id counts as one query, met by a hit to any of its families: --combine-mode all ecod:2004.1.1 PF00589 keeps contigs with some family of that T-group and PF00589.

For each kept contig, the best hit of each matched query is reported (--top-per-contig raises this). all and threshold check the queries you gave, not the biology: a contig with every marker you asked for is not proof of a complete genome, so record the exact queries with your results.

docs.title: Output files
docs.text:
File or folder Written when Content matched-contigs.fna always The contigs that passed matched-contig-ids.txt always Their ids, one per line {model}-hmmsearch-domains.tbl --keep-domtbl (default) hmmsearch per-domain table of each model .phu/query.json always, except --all-cazymes / --all-puls The query, how it was expanded and matched, and for database families the bundle version, file hashes and family names .phu/run.json --all-cazymes / --all-puls Run manifest with counts, thresholds and files written query-hmms/ database queries The models taken from the databases predicted-proteins.faa --keep-proteins Every predicted protein .phu/prediction.json --keep-proteins Where the cached proteins are and their cache key target-proteins/{model}.faa --save-target-proteins Matched proteins of each model, from kept contigs only target-hmms/{model}.hmm --save-target-hmms An HMM built from each model's matched proteins

Proteins are named <contig>|gene<n>; contig names may themselves contain |.

How models are named in output files

{model} is the model id made safe for file names (unusual characters become _). For your own HMMs in the default --hmm-mode pure, each file is one model and its file name (without extension) is the model id. If two files share a name (a/foo.hmm, b/foo.hmm), the NAME inside each HMM tells them apart; if that is identical too, phu warns and pools their hits. If two different models would get the same file name (beta/1 and beta_1), phu refuses the query rather than mix their results.

With --hmm-mode mixed, one file may hold many models (for example a concatenated or pressed database), and outputs are written per model name inside the file.

docs.title: Saving matched proteins and building HMMs
docs.text:
--save-target-proteins writes the proteins that matched each model, taken only from contigs that were kept, one file per model.

--save-target-hmms (with --save-target-proteins) builds a new HMM from each model's matched proteins: they are aligned with FAMSA and the HMM is built with pyHMMER, all inside phu. A model with a single protein gets a single-sequence HMM. Only the proteins of the current run are used.

--trim-target-msa trims each alignment with trimAl before the HMM is built:

Value What is removed none Nothing (default) gappyout Columns judged too gappy from the alignment's own gap distribution; the mildest choice strict Gappy columns and columns with low residue similarity strictplus As strict, with a tighter similarity criterion; the most aggressive

Trimming shortens the model and lowers bit scores, so cutoffs chosen for untrimmed models do not carry over. The run prints the columns before and after (gappyout: 1523 -> 377 columns). If trimming leaves no columns or fewer than two sequences, the untrimmed alignment is used, with a warning.

These HMMs are built from whatever matched, so check them before reusing them as references.

docs.title: CAZymes and PULs
docs.text:
Two options search the whole dbCAN collection instead of a query.

--all-cazymes searches every CAZyme family (AA, CBM, CE, GH, GT and PL, keeping subfamilies such as GH5_2; helper modules such as SLH, cohesin and dockerin are left out) and keeps contigs with at least one family hit.

phu-screen/
├── matched-contigs.fna
├── matched-contig-ids.txt
├── cazyme-matches.tsv.gz        # one row per contig and family
├── cazyme-family-summary.tsv    # contigs and proteins per family
├── cazyme-class-summary.tsv     # contigs and proteins per class
├── evidence/
│   └── cazyme-hits.tsv.gz       # every hit that passed
└── .phu/
    └── run.json

--all-puls checks every dbCAN-PUL signature: a contig is kept when all families of at least one PUL occur on it. Each family is searched once. PULs that name families missing from the installed dbCAN models are skipped and listed in .phu/run.json; that reflects the database, not your contigs.

phu-screen/
├── matched-contigs.fna
├── matched-contig-ids.txt
├── pul-matches.tsv.gz           # one row per contig and matched PUL
├── pul-family-support.tsv.gz    # the family hits behind each match
├── pul-summary.tsv
├── pul-substrate-summary.tsv
├── evidence/
│   └── cazyme-hits.tsv.gz
└── .phu/
    └── run.json

The CAZyme evidence is kept even when no PUL matches; the PUL tables then have only their headers. The per-family HMMs and domain tables of these runs are temporary and removed at the end.

Counts in the summaries are occurrences, not normalized abundances. The substrates in pul-substrate-summary.tsv are those annotated for the reference PULs, not predictions for your contigs. This is targeted HMM screening of CAZyme families, not a full run_dbcan annotation.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Predict proteins with pyrodigal-gv, which handles the compact genes and alternative genetic codes of phages (--mode meta, the default, for mixed contigs; single for one genome). Proteins shorter than --min-protein-len-aa are dropped. Predictions are cached and reused while the contigs and prediction settings are unchanged (see Cache handling).
  2. Search the proteins with each model using pyHMMER.
  3. Filter the hits with the cutoffs of each model's kind, then keep contigs by --combine-mode.
  4. Write the kept contigs and, if asked, their proteins and new HMMs.

Everything runs inside phu: no HMMER, seqkit or aligner program is needed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Keep contigs that carry both a major head protein and a terminase large subunit (PHROG):

phu screen -i contigs.fa --combine-mode all phrog_10 phrog_2

Keep contigs with at least 3 of 4 marker HMMs, and build new HMMs from what matched:

phu screen -i metagenome.fa --combine-mode threshold --min-hmm-hits 3 \
    --save-target-proteins --save-target-hmms \
    marker1.hmm marker2.hmm marker3.hmm marker4.hmm

Search a whole ECOD homology group, without the per-family domain tables:

phu screen -i contigs.fa --no-keep-domtbl ecod:2004.1

Be stricter, and use 16 threads:

phu screen -i contigs.fa --max-evalue 1e-10 --threads 16 protein_family.hmm

Turn off Pfam's curated cutoffs and use your own score:

phu screen -i contigs.fa --no-cut-ga --min-bitscore 30 PF00001

Quote paths that contain shell characters:

phu screen -i 'scaffolds|assembly.fa' protein_family.hmm

docs.title: simplify-taxa
docs.text:
Deprecated

phu simplify-taxa is deprecated and will be removed in a future release. It is no longer listed in phu --help, but it still runs as documented here and prints a one-line deprecation notice to stderr.

docs.title: What does it do?
docs.text: The phu simplify-taxa command converts verbose vContact taxonomy prediction values into compact lineage codes for downstream analysis. It is designed for vContact3 final_assignments.csv or TSV-style output.

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
phu simplify-taxa -i <INPUT_FILE> -o <OUTPUT_FILE> [OPTIONS]

Input and output formats are selected from their file extensions. Use --sep when the input delimiter cannot be inferred from the filename.

docs.title: Input and output
docs.text:
The command processes columns ending in _prediction, including:

  • realm_prediction
  • kingdom_prediction
  • phylum_prediction
  • class_prediction
  • order_prediction
  • family_prediction
  • subfamily_prediction
  • genus_prediction

Other columns and their order are preserved. Values that do not match a supported vContact pattern are preserved. Multiple candidate values separated by || are processed independently.

CSV output is used unless the output filename ends in .tsv; TSV output is used in that case. With --add-lineage, one additional column is appended.

docs.title: Transformation logic
docs.text:
A value such as:

novel_genus_1_of_novel_family_2_of_Caudoviricetes

becomes:

Caudoviricetes:NF2:NG1

Compact codes use these rank prefixes:

  • NK: novel kingdom
  • NP: novel phylum
  • NC: novel class
  • NO: novel order
  • NF: novel family
  • NSF: novel subfamily
  • NG: novel genus

Some vContact zero-index chains have explicit compatibility handling. Validate those version-sensitive cases against representative vContact output before using them as a scientific contract.

docs.title: Command options
docs.text:
The live CLI groups options into Input, Output, and Runtime panels. Run phu simplify-taxa --help for the current terminal menu.

 into compact codes like 'Caudoviricetes:NF2:NG1'.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Simplify a vContact CSV file:

phu simplify-taxa \
  --input-file final_assignments.csv \
  --output-file simplified.csv

Process TSV input and append the deepest available lineage:

phu simplify-taxa \
  -i final_assignments.tsv \
  -o simplified.tsv \
  --add-lineage \
  --lineage-col best_taxonomy

Override delimiter detection:

phu simplify-taxa -i assignments.txt -o simplified.csv --sep $'\t'

docs.title: Lineage column
docs.text:
The --add-lineage option appends a column containing the deepest available simplified rank. The default column name is compact_lineage; use --lineage-col to choose another name.

The priority order is:

  1. genus_prediction
  2. subfamily_prediction
  3. family_prediction
  4. order_prediction
  5. class_prediction
  6. phylum_prediction
  7. kingdom_prediction
  8. realm_prediction

docs.title: Workflow integration
docs.text:
vcontact3 --nucleotide viral-genomes.fasta --output-dir vcontact-output
phu simplify-taxa \
  -i vcontact-output/final_assignments.csv \
  -o taxonomy_simplified.csv \
  --add-lineage

The resulting table can be used for taxonomy filtering, visualization, and other downstream analyses while retaining the original input fields.
